questions.text: The Kelvin–Planck statement of the Second Law asserts that:

options.label: a
options.text: Heat cannot flow from hot to cold

options.label: b
options.text: No cyclic device can convert all the heat it absorbs into work

questions.detailed: Kelvin–Planck: it is impossible for a device operating in a cycle to convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work. Some heat must be rejected to a cold sink, so the efficiency of any heat engine is below 100%.

questions.text: The Clausius statement of the Second Law states that:

options.label: a
options.text: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a cold body to a hot body

options.label: b
options.text: Work can be fully converted to heat and back

questions.detailed: The Clausius form says heat will not of itself pass from a colder to a hotter body. Moving heat "uphill" requires work input (refrigerator/heat pump). Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements are equivalent.

questions.text: Entropy is defined for a reversible path as:
questions.detailed: $dS=\delta q_{\text{rev}}/T$. Although heat is path-dependent, $\delta q_{\text{rev}}/T$ is not — that is precisely why entropy can be defined as a state function. For an irreversible path $dS>\delta q/T$.

questions.text: The Clausius inequality is written as:
questions.detailed: $dS\ge \delta q/T$: equality holds for a reversible process, and the strict inequality $dS>\delta q/T$ for an irreversible one. Integrating over a cycle gives $\oint \delta q/T\le0$.

questions.text: For a spontaneous process in an isolated system:
questions.detailed: Spontaneous changes increase the entropy of an isolated system: $\Delta S_{\text{total}}>0$. At equilibrium $\Delta S_{\text{total}}=0$. This is the fundamental spontaneity criterion when $U$ and $V$ (or $H$ and $P$) are fixed.

questions.text: $600\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat is absorbed reversibly at a constant $300\ \mathrm{K}$. The entropy change of the system is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta S=q_{\text{rev}}/T=600/300=+2\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Entropy rises because heat enters the system.

questions.text: $1$ mol of an ideal gas expands isothermally and reversibly to double its volume. Its entropy change is (…, $R=8.314$):
questions.detailed: $\Delta S=nR\ln(V_2/V_1)=1\times8.314\times\ln2=8.314\times0.693=+5.76\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. More volume = more accessible positions = higher entropy.

questions.text: Ice melts at $273\ \mathrm{K}$ with $\Delta H_{\text{fus}}=6008\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$. The entropy of fusion is:
questions.detailed: At the melting point the process is reversible, so $\Delta S_{\text{fus}}=\Delta H_{\text{fus}}/T=6008/273\approx+22.0\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$. Melting increases disorder.

questions.text: The entropy change when a substance is heated from $T_1$ to $T_2$ at constant pressure is:
questions.detailed: From $dS=\delta q_{\text{rev}}/T$ and $\delta q_{\text{rev}}=C_P\,dT$, $\Delta S=\int_{T_1}^{T_2}(C_P/T)\,dT$. The $1/T$ factor is why entropy, not enthalpy, needs the log form.

questions.text: $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ of heat flows spontaneously from a reservoir at $500\ \mathrm{K}$ to one at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. The total entropy change is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta S=-1000/500+1000/300=-2.00+3.33=+1.33\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. Positive, confirming that hot→cold flow is spontaneous. Reversing the direction would give $-1.33\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$, forbidden by the Second Law.

questions.text: A Carnot engine operates between $500\ \mathrm{K}$ and $300\ \mathrm{K}$. Its efficiency is:
questions.detailed: $\eta_{\text{Carnot}}=1-T_c/T_h=1-300/500=0.40=40\%$. Efficiency depends only on the two reservoir temperatures, not on the working fluid.

questions.text: A Carnot engine absorbs $1000\ \mathrm{J}$ from a $600\ \mathrm{K}$ source and rejects heat at $300\ \mathrm{K}$. The work output is:
questions.detailed: $\eta=1-300/600=0.5$, so $w=\eta\,q_h=0.5\times1000=500\ \mathrm{J}$. The remaining $500\ \mathrm{J}$ is rejected to the cold sink — no engine can turn all the heat into work.

questions.text: Why can heat not be converted completely into work in a cyclic process?

options.label: b
options.text: Because the Second Law requires some heat to be rejected to a colder reservoir, so that total entropy does not decrease

options.label: c
options.text: Because heat is a state function

questions.detailed: The Kelvin–Planck statement forbids a cyclic engine from turning all absorbed heat into work; a cold sink is mandatory. Equivalently, converting all heat to work would decrease total entropy, violating the Second Law.

questions.text: For a reversible process, $\Delta S_{\text{system}}+\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}}$ equals:
questions.detailed: A reversible process produces no net entropy: $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}+\Delta S_{\text{surr}}=0$. For an irreversible (real) process the sum is strictly positive.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: White (β) tin transforms to grey (α) tin with $\Delta H=-500\ \mathrm{cal}$ at 298 K, yet white tin is the stable form at room temperature.
questions.reason: Spontaneity is decided by the total entropy change, not by the sign of $\Delta H$ alone.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: c
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: This is the classic counterexample to "negative $\Delta H$ ⇒ spontaneous." The transformation has $\Delta H<0$ but is not spontaneous at 298 K because the total entropy change (which includes the small entropy difference between the two solids) is not favourable there — it becomes spontaneous only below ~286 K, where the $T\Delta S$ term flips the free-energy sign. R is exactly why A holds.

questions.text: An ideal gas undergoes free expansion into vacuum (adiabatic, $q=0$). Its entropy change is:
questions.detailed:
Trap! The real process is irreversible, so you cannot compute $\Delta S$ from $\delta q/T$ directly. Because $S$ is a state function, replace the real path by a reversible isothermal one between the same states: $\Delta S=+nR\ln(V_2/V_1)>0$.

:::warning ⚠ Watch out
"$q=0$ so $\Delta S=0$" is wrong for an irreversible adiabatic process. Entropy is generated even though no heat flows.
:::

questions.text: Which statements are correct?

statements.text: Entropy is a state function even though it is defined via a reversible path.
The entropy change of the surroundings equals $-\Delta H_{\text{sys}}/T$ for a system at constant $T,P$.
A system's entropy can decrease if the surroundings' entropy rises even more.

questions.detailed: All three hold. Entropy is a state function (I); the heat the surroundings receive is $-\Delta H_{\text{sys}}$, so $\Delta S_{\text{surr}}=-\Delta H_{\text{sys}}/T$ at constant $T,P$ (II); and local entropy may fall so long as the total does not (III) — e.g. freezing water.

questions.text: $1$ mol of liquid water ($C_P=75.3\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}$, assumed constant) is heated from $298\ \mathrm{K}$ to $373\ \mathrm{K}$. Its entropy change is about:
Which of the following processes increases the entropy of the system?
questions.detailed: Sublimation (solid → gas) hugely increases molecular freedom and hence entropy. Freezing, condensation and ordering all reduce disorder, decreasing system entropy.

questions.text: The Second Law tells us the *direction* of spontaneous change, whereas the First Law:

options.label: b
options.text: Only accounts for energy conservation (a bookkeeping law) and says nothing about direction

options.label: c
options.text: Is a special case of the Second Law

questions.detailed: The First Law is directionless: it permits both a reaction and its reverse as long as energy balances. The Second Law supplies the arrow of time by requiring total entropy to increase.

questions.text: A block at $400\ \mathrm{K}$ and a block at $300\ \mathrm{K}$ are placed in contact with the same heat capacity. $300\ \mathrm{J}$ flows from hot to cold. The total entropy change is:
questions.detailed: $\Delta S=-300/400+300/300=-0.75+1.00=+0.25\ \mathrm{J\,K^{-1}}$. The cold block gains more entropy than the hot block loses — this net gain is the driving force for heat flow.

questions.text: For a spontaneous reaction at constant $T$ and $P$, the criterion in terms of entropy is:
questions.detailed: The correct universal criterion is $\Delta S_{\text{total}}=\Delta S_{\text{sys}}+\Delta S_{\text{surr}}\ge0$. Judging by $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}$ alone is wrong — that is why the Gibbs free energy $G$ was invented (it packages both terms using only system properties).

questions.text: "In a real (irreversible) adiabatic process the entropy of the system increases."
questions.detailed: True. Even though $q=0$, irreversibility (friction, unrestrained expansion, internal gradients) generates entropy, so $\Delta S_{\text{sys}}>0$. Entropy stays constant only if the adiabatic process is also reversible.

questions.text: The entropy of the universe in any real process:

options.label: b
options.text: Increases or stays constant, never decreases

options.label: d
options.text: Can be made to decrease with a catalyst

questions.detailed: $\Delta S_{\text{universe}}\ge0$: it increases for irreversible processes and stays constant for ideal reversible ones. No process can lower it.

questions.text: Which best describes the physical meaning of entropy?

options.label: a
options.text: The total energy of the system

options.label: b
options.text: A measure of energy dispersal / the number of accessible microscopic states

options.label: c
options.text: The heat capacity at constant volume

questions.detailed: Entropy measures how widely energy is dispersed and, statistically, $S=k_B\ln\Omega$ — the number of accessible microstates. Higher entropy means more ways to arrange the system at the same energy.

questions.text: Spontaneity at constant $T$ and $V$ is governed by the Helmholtz free energy $A=U-TS$. Which condition means spontaneous?
questions.detailed: At constant $T,V$ the system tends to minimise $A$, so $\Delta A<0$ is spontaneous and $\Delta A=0$ is equilibrium. (At constant $T,P$ the analogous function is $G$.)
